G9100.d: 1. to look about, look carefully , followed by preposition εἰς, (Odyssey by Homer):—;with accusative to look after, watch , (Iliad by Homer), attic:—;absolute to look out, reconnoitre , (Herdotus Historicus); σκέψαι look , (Aeschulus Tragicus); σκέψασθε look out , (Aristophanes Comicus) 2. of the mind, to look to, view, examine, consider, think on , (Sophocles Tragicus), etc.:—; σκέψασθε δέ: only consider , (Thucydides) 3. to think of beforehand, premeditate , (Demosthenes Orator) 4. perfect also in passive sense, ἐσκεμμένα things well-considered , (Thucydides); σκοπεῖτε οὖν. Answ. ἔσκεπται (Plato Philosophus); so 3 future passive ἐσκέψεται (Plato Philosophus) (ML)

G9104.d: 1. a staff or stick to lean upon, a walking-stick , (Homer): metaphorically of the daughters of Oedipus, σκῆπτρα φωτός his staffs or supports , (Sophocles Tragicus) 2. a staff , as the badge of command, a sceptre : in (Homer) borne by chiefs, and transmitted from father to son, whence the passage in (Iliad by Homer) 2 is called ἡ τοῦ σκήπτρου παράδοσις, (Thucydides):—;also borne by judges, by heralds, by speakers, who on rising to speak received it from the herald, (Homer) 3. the sceptre , i. e. royalty, kingly power, rule , [8th/7th c.BC, variant datesTragica Adespota (ML)

G9106.d: 1. to overshadow, shade , (Iliad by Homer) 2. generally, to overshadow, cover , (Hesiod):—;Pass., (Euripides) 3. to shade in painting , (Lucian) (ML)

G9112.d: crookedness , (Plutarch): in plural the windings of a stream, etc., (Strabo Geographus) (ML)

G9115.d: 1. a lookout-place, a mountain-peak , (Homer): of the Trojan acropolis, (Euripides): compare σκόπελος. 2. metaphorically the height or highest point of anything, (Pindar) 3. a watchtower , Lat. specula, (Herdotus Historicus) 4. a look-out, watch , σκοπιὴν ἔχειν to keep watch , (Odyssey by Homer) (ML)

G9119.d: to look angry or sullen, be of a sad countenance , (Aristophanes Comicus), etc. from σκυθρωπός (ML)

G9120.d: 1. to strip or despoil a slain enemy of his arms, (Hesiod); with accusative of persons or things, Κύκνον σκυλεύσαντες ἀπp ὤμων τεύχεα having stript the arms of Cycnus from his shoulders, (Hesiod) 2. with accusative rei et genitive pers. to strip the arms off an enemy, (Xenophon Historicus); so, ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν σκ. ψέλια (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G9121.d: a cub, whelp , especially a lion's whelp , (Iliad by Homer), attic; of other animals, (Euripides); in poets also of men, Ἀχίλλειος σκ. (Euripides) (ML)

G9122.d: 1. a staff, cudgel, club , [variant datesAnthology Palantina 2. at Sparta, a staff or baton , used as a cypher for writing dispatches:—;a strip of leather was rolled slantwise round it, on which the dispatches were written lengthwise, so that when unrolled they were unintelligible: commanders abroad had a staff of like thickness, round which they rolled these papers, and so were able to read the dispatches:—;hence σκυτάλη came to mean a Spartan dispatch , (Thucydides); and generally a message , (Pindar) derivation uncertain (ML)

G9127.d: 1. Lat. taxus, the yew, (Plato Philosophus) 2. the convolvulus , or perhaps bryony , [variant datesTragica Adespota, (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)

G9130.d: 1. a master of one's craft or art, an adept , of a diviner, (Herdotus Historicus); of poets, (Pindar); of the Creator, (Plato Philosophus); metaphorically, ς. πημάτων an adept in misery, (Euripides) 2. like φρόνιμος, one who is clever in matters of life, a wise man , in which sense the seven Sages are called σοφισταί, (Herdotus Historicus); of Prometheus, (Aeschulus Tragicus) 3. at Athens, a Sophist , i. e. a professor of grammar, rhetoric, politics, mathematics, such as Prodicus, Gorgias, Protagoras, (Thucydides), etc. At first the Sophists were held in honour; but from their loose principles they fell into ill repute, and the word came to mean, 4. a sophist (in bad sense), a quibbler, cheat , (Aristophanes Comicus), etc. (ML)

G9134.d: 1. of things, to be rare, scarce, scanty , (Pindar) 2. of persons, to lack or be in want of , τινός (Herdotus Historicus), etc.;—;so in Pass., ἐσπανίσμεθ᾽ ἀρωγῶν (Aeschulus Tragicus): absolute to be in want , (Euripides) (ML)

G9135.d: 1. rare, scarce, scanty , (Herdotus Historicus); σπάνιον ἑαυτὸν παρέχειν, Lat. difficiles aditus habere, (Plato Philosophus); ὕδατι σπανίῳ χρώμενοι having a scanty supply of water, (Thucydides); with infinitive, σπ. ἰδεῖν rare to behold, (Xenophon Historicus): of persons in an adverb sense, σπάνιος ἐπιφοιτᾷ he seldom visits, (Herdotus Historicus):—; σπάνιόν ἐστι, with infinitive, it is seldom that . ., (Xenophon Historicus):—; τὸ σπάνιον = σπάνις, (Aeschines Orator) 2. comparative σπανιώτερος, (Herdotus Historicus): —;Sup. -ώτατος, attic 3. adverb -ίως, seldom , (Xenophon Historicus); so σπανίᾳ, (Plato Philosophus): comparative -ιώτερον, (Thucydides) (ML)

G9136.d: a swathing band , and in plural swaddling-clothes , (Homeric Hymns); παῖς ἔτ᾽ ὢν ἐν σπαργάνοις (Aeschulus Tragicus); tokens by which a person is identified , Lat. monumenta, crepundia, (Sophocles Tragicus) (ML)

G9140.d: the space one can span with the thumb and little finger, a span , Lat. dodrans, about 7 1/2 inches , (Herdotus Historicus) derivation uncertain (ML)

G9141.d: a spark , Lat. scintilla, (Iliad by Homer) (ML)

G9142.d: 1. a heap of ashes, ashes , (Odyssey by Homer) 2. metaphorically, = σποδός III, [variant datesAnthology Palantina (ML)

G9145.d: 1. a drink-offering , i. e. the wine poured out to the gods before drinking, Lat. libatio, (Hesiod); σπονδὰς θεοῖς λείβειν, σπένδειν (Aeschulus Tragicus) 2. in plural, σπονδαί was a solemn treaty or truce , (because solemn drink-offerings were made on concluding them); σπονδαὶ ἄκρητοι the truce made by pouring unmixed wine, (Iliad by Homer); αἱ Λακεδαιμονίων σπ. the truce with them. (Thucydides); σπονδὰς παραδιδόναι (Aristophanes Comicus); δέχεσθαι (Thucydides); τυχεῖν (Xenophon Historicus); σπ. ποιεῖσθαί τινι to make a truce with one, (Herdotus Historicus); πρός τινα (Aristophanes Comicus); σπ. τέμνειν (like ὅρκια τέμνειν); (Euripides); σπ. ἄγειν πρός τινας (Thucydides) 3. αἱ Ὀλυμπικαὶ σπ. the solemn truce or armistice during the Olympic games, (Thucydides) 4. the treaty itself , εἴρηται ἐν ταῖς σπ. (Thucydides) (ML)

G9147.d: 1. of persons, 2. with accusative rei, to drop, let fall or shed drop by drop , (Iliad by Homer), etc. 3. with dative rei, αἵματι στ. to drip with blood, (Aeschulus Tragicus); στάζων ἱδρῶτι (Sophocles Tragicus);—;rarely with genitive, (Aeschulus Tragicus) 4. intransitive of things, to drop, fall in drops, drip, trickle , (Herdotus Historicus); metaphorically, στάζει ἐν ὕπνωι πόνος (Aeschulus Tragicus) (ML)

G9148.d: 1. to measure by rule , (Euripides): —;Pass., with future middle -ήσομαι, to be measured, estimated , (Aristophanes Comicus) 2. as Dep. (see. σταθμόω); to estimate distance or size, without actual measurement, (Herdotus Historicus): metaphorically to estimate one thing by another, τί τινι (Plato Philosophus); absolute to conjecture , (Sophocles Tragicus) 3. to attach weight to a thing, value it, (Plato Philosophus) (ML)

G9150.d: 1. a standing place for animals, Lat. stabulum, a stable, fold, (Iliad by Homer): a stye , (Odyssey by Homer): of men, a dwelling, abode , (Hesiod) 2. quarters, lodgings for travellers or soldiers, Lat. statio, (Xenophon Historicus) 3. in Persia, σταθμοί were stations on the royal road, where the king rested, (Herdotus Historicus): hence a day's journey, day's march , averaging about 5 parasangs or 15 miles, (Herdotus Historicus) 4. like Lat. statio, a station for ships, (Euripides) 5. an upright post, the bearing pillar of the roof, (Odyssey by Homer): a door-post , especially in plural, (Homer), attic 6. the balance , (Aristophanes Comicus); ἱστᾶν σταθμῷ τι πρός τι to weigh one thing against another, (Herdotus Historicus) 7. weight , σταθμὸν ἔχειν τάλαντον to weigh a talent, (Herdotus Historicus); absolute in accusative, ἴσα σταθμόν equal in weight , (Herdotus Historicus); ἡμιπλίνθια σταθμὸν διτάλαντα two talents in or by weight , (Herdotus Historicus):—;in plural weights , (Euripides), etc. (ML)

G9151.d: flour of spelt mixed and made into dough , (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G9155.d: stiff fat, tallow, suet , Lat. sebum, opp. toπιμελή (Lat. adeps, soft fat), (Odyssey by Homer) (ML)

G9157.d: to cover , (Xenophon Historicus): metaphorically, ὕπνος στ. τινά covers, embraces one, (Sophocles Tragicus):—;Pass., πλοῖον ἐστεγασμένον a decked vessel, (Antipho Orator) (ML)

G9158.d: 1. waterproof , (Herdotus Historicus); στεγνὰ οἰκήματα, of a cave, (Euripides) 2. as Substantive, στεγνόν, οῦ, a covered dwelling , (Xenophon Historicus) (ML)

G9159.d: the crown of the root, stump , whence the trunk springs, Lat. codex, (Pindar) (ML)

G9160.d: a mass of olives from which the oil has been pressed, olive-cake , (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)

G9161.d: 1. to be mourned, giving cause for grief , (Sophocles Tragicus) 2. mournful , (Euripides) (ML)

G9162.d: 1. to moan, sigh, groan , (Homer) 2. with genitive to moan or sigh for , (Euripides); ὑπέρ τινος (Aeschulus Tragicus); τινί or ἐπί τινι (Euripides); with accusative cognate, πένθος οἰκεῖον στ. (Sophocles Tragicus):—;Mid., (Aeschulus Tragicus) 3. with accusative to bewail, lament , (Aeschulus Tragicus), etc.; στένειν τινὰ τῆς τύχης to pity him for his ill fortune, (Aeschulus Tragicus): so in Mid., στένεσθαί τινα (Euripides) (ML)

G9166.d: 1. to deprive, bereave, rob of anything, with accusative pers. et genitive rei, (Odyssey by Homer), attic 2. with accusative rei, to take away , [variant datesAnthology Palantina:—;Pass. to have taken from one , βίον στερείς (Euripides) (ML)

G9167.d: to deprive of a thing, (Thucydides):—;Pass. to be deprived of a thing, (Herdotus Historicus), attic (ML)

G9168.d: 1. anything that encircles the head, for defence or ornament: 2. the brim of the helmet, projecting behind as well as before, (Iliad by Homer) 3. part of a woman's head-dress, a diadem, coronal , (Iliad by Homer), etc.:—;metaphorically, of a city, ἀπὸ στεφάναν κέκαρσαι πύργων thou hast been shorn of thy coronal of towers, (Euripides) 4. the brim or edge of anything, the brow of a hill, edge of a cliff , (Iliad by Homer); of a basket, (Moschus Bucolicus) (ML)

G9171.d: 1. a block of stone used as a prop or buttress to a wall , (Iliad by Homer): a block of rockcrystal, in which the Egyptian mummies were cased, (Herdotus Historicus) 2. a block or slab , bearing an inscription; and so, 3. a gravestone , (Homer), attic 4. a block or slab , inscribed with record of victories, dedications, treaties, decrees, etc., (Herdotus Historicus), attic; γράφειν τινὰ εἰς στήλην, ἀναγράφειν ἐν στήλῃ, whether for honour, or for infamy, (Herdotus Historicus):—;also the record itself, a contract, agreement , κατὰ τὴν στήλην according to agreement , (Aristophanes Comicus); στῆλαι αἱ πρὸς Θηβαίους (Demosthenes Orator) 5. a boundary post, (Xenophon Historicus):—; the turning-post at the end of the racecourse, Lat. meta, (Sophocles Tragicus) 6. for Στῆλαι Ἡρακλήιαι, see. Ἡράκλειος. (ML)

G9173.d: to set up as a monument , [variant datesAnthology Palantina (ML)

G9175.d: 1. the warp in the ancient upright loom, (Hesiod) 2. a thread , (Batrachomyomachia) (ML)

G9180.d: Mid. or Pass. to paint one's eyelids and eyebrows with black paint στίβι); (Strabo Geographus) (ML)

G9181.d: punctured , [variant datesAnthology Palantina:—;generally, spotted, dappled , (Sophocles Tragicus); στικτὰ ὄμματα, of the hundred eyes of Argus, (Euripides) (ML)

G9184.d: 1. a row or file of soldiers, (Xenophon Historicus) 2. a line of poetry, a verse , (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)

G9186.d: a plant used for stuffing or padding; and metaphorically " padding , " an expletive , (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)

G9187.d: 1. to set a row of poles with nets to drive the game into, (Xenophon Historicus) 2. to order or arrange in system , (Aeschulus Tragicus) (ML)

G9188.d: 1. to put in trim , στολίσας νηὸς πτερά having trimmed the sails, (Hesiod) 2. to equip, dress :—;Pass., ἐστολισμένος δορί armed with spear, (Euripides) 3. metaphorically to deck, adorn , [variant datesAnthology Palantina (ML)

G9191.d: 1. to aim or shoot at , with genitive, τοῦ σκοποῦ (Plato Philosophus), etc. 2. metaphorically to aim at, endeavour after , (Plato Philosophus); στ. φίλων κριτῶν to aim at having friends as judges, (Xenophon Historicus) 3. to endeavour to make out, to guess at a thing, with genitive, (Isocrates Orator):—; absolute to make guesses, conjecture, (Sophocles Tragicus) (ML)

G9198.d: 1. to encamp, bivouac, take up a position , (Xenophon Historicus): 2. as Dep. στρατοπεδεύομαι, (Herdotus Historicus), etc.; perfect ἐστρατοπεδεῦσθαι to be in camp , (Xenophon Historicus): of a fleet, to be stationed , (Herdotus Historicus) (ML)

G9199.d: twisted, crooked , (Aristotle Philosopher); of the brows, knit, wrinkled , [variant datesAnthology Palantina: metaphorically, στρεβλοῖσι παλαίσμασι by cunning dodges in wrestling, (Aristophanes Comicus) (ML)
